title: Each number pops once
hook: Is "next bigger" a scan from every position?

doesNotKnow: that a stack of still-waiting values answers "next bigger to the right" in one pass

misconception: Finding the next bigger number for every position needs a scan to the right from each position: about n^2 checks.
objective: The learner can explain that a stack of numbers still waiting for a bigger one answers 'next bigger to the right' in one pass, because each number is pushed once and popped at most once: on 9 8 ... 1 it costs 8 comparisons against the scan's 36, and on 8 ... 1 9 it costs 15 even though the 9 pops eight numbers at once.

claims.text: On 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1, scanning right from each position until a bigger number costs 36 comparisons (8 + 7 + ... + 1); none of them has a bigger number to its right.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run() (scanTotal), the number the question and stage print. Builder's node script (2026-10-14): 36. Closed form 8·9/2 = 36. Convention: the scan from position i compares a[i] with a[i+1], a[i+2], ... and stops at the first bigger value or the end.

claims.text: With a stack of values still waiting, 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 costs 8 comparisons: each new number is compared once with the top, which is bigger, and pushed.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run() (stackTotal). Convention (disclosed in the Demo.tsx header): a stack comparison is one test of the new value against the current top; the first number meets an empty stack and costs nothing. Builder's node script (2026-10-14): 8 comparisons, 0 pops.

claims.text: On 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 9, scanning still costs 36, and the stack costs 15: 7 comparisons while the first eight are pushed, then 8 as the 9 pops all eight waiting numbers; each of the eight gets the answer 9 and the 9 gets none.
claims.source: List added by the spec (company/design/specs/each-element-pops-once.md), not in the brief. Demo.tsx run() on LISTS[1]; builder's node script (2026-10-14): scan 36, stack 15, 8 pops, answers 9 9 9 9 9 9 9 9 none. 9 pushes + 8 pops = 17 <= 18.

claims.text: A number waits on the stack until a bigger one arrives, and then it is popped and answered, exactly once.
claims.source: The stack holds indices whose next bigger value has not been seen yet, in decreasing value from bottom to top; when a[i] arrives every smaller top is popped and answered with a[i], the first bigger value to its right (anything between them was smaller, else it would have popped it first). Each index is pushed once, so popped at most once.

claims.text: Every stack comparison either pops a number or ends that number's turn, so 9 numbers cost at most 9 pushes and 9 pops: the work grows like n, not n².
claims.source: Amortised (aggregate) count: comparisons <= pops + (n - 1), pops <= n, so comparisons < 2n; pushes + pops <= 2n. The aggregate method is CLRS 4e chapter 16 (amortized analysis; its stack MULTIPOP example uses the same argument). Scanning costs up to n(n-1)/2 (c1).

recall.question: A one-pass stack answers 'next bigger to the right' for 1,000 numbers. At most about how many stack comparisons can it make?
recall.why: Each number is pushed once and popped at most once, and every comparison either pops a number or ends a turn, so the work is under 2 x 1,000. Scanning from every position can cost about 500,000.
